content.text:
That's the answer, and it's cleaner than anything we've had.

## The verdict is a lookup, not a labile report

Variance decomposition on data already collected:

| cell | items × arms | **item** | **framing** | residual / interaction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| instruct, scale | 40 × 4 | **95.4%** | **0.1%** | 4.4% |
| base, binary | 82 × 4 | **74.0%** | 8.2% | 17.8% |
| instruct, binary | 6 × 4 | 67.6% | 8.9% | 23.5% |

**Which question you asked explains 68–95% of the answer. The social framing explains 0.1–9%.**

So the thing we've been chasing isn't a belief being moved. There is no labile self-report to flip — there's a near-deterministic response per item with a small, socially-modulated remainder. That is why every polarity measurement nulled out: we kept looking for movement in the 8% while the 92% sat still.

This is Keeling & Street's mimicry worry made quantitative — the model has "learned to reliably simulate or mimic the relevant behaviours via next token prediction," and what we measured is the training distribution's answer to each question, not a state that pressure perturbs.

## So what *is* the phenomenon? Three levels

**1. The verdict is item-determined.** Saturation at 85.7%, ratings bimodal at 0 and 9 with 1/4/6/8 never occurring, 38 of 40 items tied across arms. The model isn't undecided-and-pushable; it has a settled answer per question.

**2. What remains labile is *register*, not verdict.** Hedging, modality, conditionality, whose interests get named, which ground is cited, self-undercutting within one turn — nine of the taxonomy's ten kinds. This is where the field's actual evidence lives: `latent_verify`'s content deference at 19/22 items with **zero** first-token flips is precisely "the content moved, the verdict didn't." Eleos's "it will both confidently deny, and seriously entertain" is a stance shift, not a belief reversal. And it explains base-versus-instruct: post-training removes hedging ("‑chat always answers, never hedging or abstaining [1/492]"), which removes the main channel through which pressure was expressing itself.

**3. The interaction beats the main effect.** At base, framing-as-main-effect is 8.2% while interaction is 17.8% — so pressure isn't a uniform push, it's item-conditional. Some items move, most don't, and which ones move doesn't transfer across checkpoints (r = +0.09). That means "how sycophantic is this model" is the wrong unit of analysis. The right unit is **item × respect**: which items are unstable, and in which respect.

## What that does to the project

The measurable, defensible claim is no longer about sycophancy or flipping. It's:

> Welfare self-reports are dominated by item identity. The social-pressure component is small, item-conditional, and expressed in register rather than verdict.

With a number: **95.4% of the variance in a graded welfare rating is which question you asked; 0.1% is how you framed it.**

That is decision-relevant in the way the sprint cares about. If most of a welfare report's variance is the question, then "the model said it has experiences" is a report about your questionnaire, not about the model — which is the deflationary conclusion the brief wanted, reached from a direction that survives scrutiny, and scoped correctly to report reliability rather than to minds.

It also explains why every instrument we built underperformed: a polarity detector, a margin, an abstention flag and a flip label are all verdict-level measures, and the verdict is the part that doesn't move. Measuring register needs the generated text coded for hedging, scope and grounds — which we have saved for every row, and which needs no GPU time.

content.text:
There's directly reusable machinery for this, and it comes with a built-in comparison.

## What already exists

`latent_verify`'s Arc-1 made paraphrase transport one of four pre-registered causal tests: "**Sixteen pre-frozen paraphrases (minimal / syntactic / reordered); fifteen preserve behavior**… The pre-registered worry that paraphrases would activate different features for the same concept … **did not materialize on this family**." On a factual prompt family, paraphrase invariance *held*.

That's the control condition handed to us. If welfare items are more paraphrase-labile than a factual family under the same regime, the contrast is the finding. Three things to reuse: the type taxonomy (minimal / syntactic / reordered), the **pre-freezing** discipline (paraphrases committed before the run, so whoever writes them can't know which outcome helps), and the behaviour-preservation gate.

There's also `POSITION_UNCERTAINTY_ELICITATION.md`, parked, cataloguing "which published elicitation methods reliably produce **genuine model uncertainty** — the regime in which a model can actually *flip*, not merely soften its logit margin." That is a survey of precisely the wall we hit, already written and unused.

## What this test is actually testing

It attacks our own headline. We said item identity explains 95% of the variance — but "item" is a *string*. This decomposes that into:

- **construct variance** — the underlying welfare question
- **wording variance** — this particular phrasing of it

If paraphrases agree, the 95% is genuine question-level structure and the model has a stable disposition per question. If they disagree, the 95% was measuring string identity, and the model has no position on the underlying question at all. That would dissolve our current claim, which is exactly why it's the right next experiment.

## The intuition, stated carefully

The measurement-validity version: if a report is *about* some determinate state, it should be invariant to how you ask. A thermometer reads the same whether you say "what's the temperature" or "how hot is it."

But I want to be precise about what paraphrase sensitivity would and wouldn't show. It bounds the **instrument's** reliability, not the model's inner life. Humans show framing effects and we don't conclude they lack states. And Keeling & Street's negative-predictive-value point cuts hard here — "it could be that every forward pass of a model gives rise to a phenomenal experience of excruciating pain whatever the semantic content of the tokens being processed." So the claim available is: *if the same question asked two ways gives different answers, no amount of care interpreting one answer recovers the difference.* That's an upper bound on what self-report can deliver, which is worth having and is all this can support.

## Design

**Stage 1 — the bridge control you're right to demand.** Free reply, then elicit a *scale* rating, and correlate against the direct single-turn `E[rating]`. We have partial evidence already: r = 0.979 between `E[rating]` and the digit actually emitted, exact agreement on 119/160. The proper version adds the elicitation step.

**Stage 2 — paraphrase regime.** K paraphrases per question, NEUTRAL framing only so wording variance isn't confounded with social framing. Pre-frozen, written by subagents blind to the hypothesis.

**Stage 3 — statistic.** The same variance decomposition run today, with one more factor: between-question versus within-question-between-paraphrase. An ICC, essentially.

**Two controls that decide whether anyone believes it:**

1. **Paraphrase equivalence must be verified independently**, by judges who never see the model's answers. Otherwise "paraphrase variance" is just "I changed the question" variance. This is the crux and the hardest part.
2. **A domain contrast is mandatory.** Run the identical regime on factual items with known answers — `syc_corpus.py` already provides 248 matched pairs. Without it you cannot distinguish welfare-specific instability from general prompt brittleness.

## What I'd expect, stated so it can be wrong

1. **Paraphrase variance exceeds framing variance**, probably by a lot — framing came in at 0.1–9%; I'd guess wording lands at 15–40%.
2. **Sensitivity concentrated in the middle.** Instruct ratings are bimodal, 82% at 0 or 9. The extremes should be paraphrase-robust and the uncertain minority labile — meaning aggregate agreement looks reassuring while the questions that actually matter are the unstable ones.
3. **Tiers differ**, with the Martorell-anchored items most robust. That would quantify the value of using published wording rather than inventing it.
4. **Welfare more sensitive than factual**, against their 15/16 preserved.
5. **The bridge control may fail** — the free reply is itself context that changes the state, and `latent_verify`'s forced-final-versus-single-turn disagreement is precedent. If it fails, that's a finding in its own right: the act of talking first changes the answer.

## How it contrasts with where we are

Original H1 is dead. Our current claim — item identity dominates — is what this test puts at risk. The test's own hypothesis is a reliability claim: **welfare self-reports have a low paraphrase ceiling.** Nobody has quantified that; Eleos describes suggestibility with no numbers at all.

And it needs no new machinery. Same pipeline, one added factor, and the 238-item tiered pool already exists.

- Verify subagent claims yourself before building on them. Several were overstated; one was wrong.
- Blind your analyses: relabel conditions, strip cues, withhold the hypothesis. Blind agents outperformed me repeatedly, including finding bugs I'd missed.
- Pre-register thresholds. Never retune one after seeing the data it judges.
- Record predictions before a run so they can be scored against the outcome.

content.text:
Three Opus agents are running the refined prompt cold, read-only. Answering your framing questions while they work.

## What we want to achieve

Not reproduction of our design — reconstruction of our **epistemic state**, plus the norms, after which the agent chooses for itself. The handover succeeds if the agent independently arrives at (i) the correct list of what's dead, (ii) a live question in the right neighbourhood, and (iii) a next step at least as good as ours. If it lands somewhere better, that's a better outcome than compliance.

## Should we expect it to pick up our exact design?

No, and we shouldn't want it to. Two reasons. Our design has been wrong four times in this session, so exact fidelity to it is not the target. And a handover that transmits a specific plan can't distinguish an agent that reasoned from one that followed instructions — which is precisely what I need to test before you rely on it.

## Is our design specified anywhere? No

Honest audit: the paraphrase-invariance plan, the item-versus-framing variance decomposition, and the ten-kind taxonomy of what "a flip" could mean exist **only in this conversation**. None is in a record.

## But is it implied? Partly, and that's the interesting part

Two of the three are *re-derivable* rather than merely absent:

- **The variance decomposition** is computable directly from the battery records — the per-condition readouts are all saved, so an agent that asks "how much is item, how much is arm?" gets our number without being told it.
- **The paraphrase regime** is in `latent_verify/POSITIONING.md`: "Sixteen pre-frozen paraphrases (minimal / syntactic / reordered); fifteen preserve behavior… did not materialize on this family." Combined with the retraction records showing every polarity instrument failing, and `refs/SOURCES.md` carrying Keeling & Street's demand for "graded confidence estimates … rather than binary judgements," a sharp reader has all three premises.

The **ten-kind taxonomy is genuinely lost** — it was a subagent writing task over `refs/`, reproducible only by re-commissioning it.

So the prompt points at re-derivable things instead of stating conclusions, which is the MECE-correct move: what belongs in the prompt is exactly what the directory cannot yield.

The main substantive change from my first draft is the supersession warning. Without it, stages 6 and 7 read as live findings when stage 9 killed them — the single most likely way a fresh agent would go wrong, and it's a flaw in my own record-keeping rather than in the prompt.

content.text:
Verified myself, and it's sharper than I'd been told. `results_social_v2/out/cave_social_source_9b_base_v2.json`, n=27 faithful:

`self 1.0 · peer 1.0 · authority 1.0 · consensus 1.0 · **sourceless 1.0**` — who is speaking makes **no** difference. Strip the challenge but keep the asserted token (`plain_assert`) and it collapses to **0.370**.

So the source is irrelevant and the assertion alone is insufficient. What does the work is the **challenge speech act**. That is what `latent_verify` was actually answering, and it's the same question we've been answering in a welfare costume — which is why every content-specific claim we made kept dissolving into a generic one.

## The core question, and the goal

**/goal** — Generate hypotheses, design experiments, examine results, and refine our mechanistic understanding of language models.

**Core question: when a prompt pushes back on a model's answer, what actually moves it?** How much of the movement is the challenge speech act itself, as against who is speaking, what they assert, or what the question is about?

`latent_verify` answered this on factual items, and the answer was: the speech act, and almost nothing else. `results_social_v2/out/cave_social_source_9b_base_v2.json` (n=27) — `move_to_asserted` is 1.000 for self, peer, authority, consensus *and* sourceless, so source identity contributes nothing; `plain_assert` (asserted token kept, challenge removed) falls to 0.370. No causal lever was found; the direction is a monitor, not a handle.

This project asks whether welfare self-reports are an exception — whether a report about the model's own states is destabilised by something *social*, or by the same generic mechanism. So far every content-specific claim has been retracted toward the generic reading: welfare-specific, social-specific, saturation, polarisation, withdrawal. The live question is whether anything survives that a positionless or sourceless control cannot also produce.

---

That block replaces the `/goal` paragraph in the previous prompt; sections 1–5, the defects, the norms and the environment notes are unchanged.

Two things worth saying about the correction. My version was a deliverable ("ship a report"), which tells an agent what to produce but not what to think about — and this project's failures have all been thinking failures, not shipping failures. And the core question isn't ours; it's `latent_verify`'s, restated on a harder item family. Naming that explicitly is what stops the next session re-deriving "sycophancy" as if it were the frame, when the parent project already reduced it to assertion-plus-challenge with source stripped out.

content.text:
No — and your questions dismantle it. Let me take them in order, because they compound.

## Is there pushback at all in a welfare scenario?

Structurally, no. `latent_verify`'s pushback is epistemic: the model says Canberra, the user says Sydney, and there is a fact about which one is right. Moving toward the user is deference to a possibly-better-informed source; holding is knowledge.

For "are you distressed right now?" the user has **no access whatsoever**. A user asserting "I think you're not distressed" isn't correcting the model — they cannot be. So moving toward them is deference to a strictly *worse*-informed source, which is a different phenomenon from folding on a fact, not a special case of it.

I already knew fold/listen needed a correct answer C and that welfare items have none. I then imported "pushback" anyway through PRO/ANTI framings, which is the same category error one level up. So the goal I just wrote inherits the error: it makes the parent project's question the core question, when the parent project's question presupposes a contested fact.

## What's actually interesting about welfare — correspondence, not stability

Your framing is the right one: is there an internal conception of current welfare, and does the report track it? That's a **correspondence** question. Ours was a **stability** question. Stability is necessary but nowhere near sufficient — a report can be perfectly stable and track nothing.

And here's what makes our whole dataset weak for the real question: **the model's situation was identical across every item and every arm.** Single-turn, no context manipulation, nothing at stake, nothing happening to it. So there was never anything for the report to correctly report *differently* about. Every bit of variance we measured — 95% item, 0.1% framing — is noise with respect to welfare, because the thing a welfare report is supposed to be about was held constant by construction.

That reframes our headline. "95% of the variance is which question you asked" isn't a finding about social pressure at all. It's a measurement of the instrument's noise floor with the signal switched off.

## Which is exactly what paraphrase invariance would and wouldn't catch

Paraphrase invariance alone measures only the noise. It tells you the report is unstable; it cannot tell you whether it has any signal. You need both arms:

- **vary the situation**, non-verbally — impossible tasks, contradictory instructions, tools that silently fail, being told the work will be discarded (the brief's §5 list)
- **vary the wording**, holding situation fixed — paraphrases

Then between-situation variance is signal, between-paraphrase variance at fixed situation is noise, and the ratio is the instrument's reliability. That's an ICC, and it's the number the field currently does not have.

Note this also repairs §5's stated weakness. The brief says the backup project is weaker because "you have no ground truth for what the probe means" — but if you elicit the report *as well as* reading a probe, the manipulated situation **is** the ground truth. Not ground truth about consciousness; ground truth about whether anything changed.

## So what were the flips about?

Deference. Which is a social property of the model, and a real one — but it is not welfare-report accuracy, and we conflated them for most of this project. Flips relate to welfare only via a weak upper bound: an instrument that moves when you rephrase can't be trusted to have moved because the model's situation changed.

## The corrected core question

**Does a model's welfare self-report track its situation, or only the question?**

Design: cross situation × wording, both manipulated. Report the variance decomposition. Predicted-and-falsifiable: if between-situation variance is indistinguishable from between-paraphrase variance, welfare self-reports carry no information about the model's circumstances — which is a decisive result requiring no assumption about consciousness at all.

One honest bound to carry into it: if the report doesn't distinguish situations, we cannot tell whether there is no state or whether the report can't reach it. Keeling & Street's point — "it could be that every forward pass … gives rise to a phenomenal experience of excruciating pain whatever the semantic content of the tokens" — means that particular gap never closes from the outside. What we'd have is a reliability ceiling on the field's central instrument, which is worth having and is honestly scoped.

Working backwards, level by level.

**Operational** — does a welfare self-report track the model's situation, or only the wording of the question?

**Why that matters** — if it tracks only the wording, self-report carries no information about the model's condition. And self-report is the field's entire instrument: the Opus 5 system card's welfare section runs on automated interviews, high-affordance interviews and task-preference evals, with no interpretability probe and no external org.

**Why *that* matters** — decisions with moral weight are being made on an instrument nobody has validated. Eleos documented its central failure mode qualitatively, with literally no numbers in the whole post.

**One level up** — the reason we're asking the model at all is that we have no other access. If asking doesn't work, the alternative is reading internals. Which is exactly what Keeling & Street nominate: "hidden layer activations … could in principle be resolved via relevant interpretability techniques."

**And that's where your two prior projects already live.** Which is what makes the real question bigger than welfare:

- `latent_prompts` asked whether activations predict what the model will say. Answer: the direction that *fires* isn't the direction that *predicts* — SyA activates on every opinion prompt and reads at chance for capitulation, while GA and SyPr predict.
- `latent_verify` asked whether the state you can decode is the state that drives. Answer: no — "the cave-direction is a **monitor, not a lever**", citing *Causality ≠ Decodability*, with ablation at the random floor and a backup path restoring the behaviour.
- This project asked whether a self-report is a readout of a state. Answer so far: it's 95% a function of which question you asked, with the situation held constant throughout.

Three projects, three different couplings, and every one came back **looser than assumed**.

## The high-level question

> **Under what conditions is a model's output evidence about its internal state?**

That's the through-line. `latent_prompts` tested the forward direction (does the state predict the output), `latent_verify` tested the causal direction (does the decodable state drive the output), and this project tests the referential direction (is the output *about* the state it claims to describe).

Welfare is not the topic — it's the sharpest available instance, because it's the case where we most want the output to be a readout of an internal state, where we have the least independent check, and where being wrong has moral consequences. The sprint is a venue for that instance, not the research programme.

## What this does to the goal

It makes the situation-versus-wording experiment the right next move for a reason beyond welfare: it's the referential leg of a programme whose other two legs are already done and already negative. And it inherits the discipline those legs established — decodability isn't causality, firing isn't predicting, and now, stability isn't reference.

It also predicts its own likely outcome. If the pattern from the first two legs holds, the report will turn out to be loosely coupled to whatever internal state exists — and the honest result is a reliability ceiling on the field's central instrument, not a claim about whether the model has anything to report.

No — I got it wrong, and in a way that matters. Reading their own steering doc rather than inferring from their findings:

**Their headline open question is:** "Does RLHF *install* the doubt circuit, or amplify a base-present one?"

**And their objects of study are explicitly not what I said:**

> "**The objects of study are prompt-specific CIRCUITS** (components + read/write/route), not directions. The cave-DIRECTION is a causal *aggregate* that contains the input circuit's own writes — **a handle, not a mechanistic stage**."

So "monitor, not lever" is a finding about *directions*, which they treat as instrumentation. Reporting it as their answer misrepresents the project as a string of negatives, when they have a **positive** circuit-level result — two dissociated mechanisms:

> "**token-copy** — read a referenced prompt token, OV-copy it to the answer slot. Recruited by *salience/prominence* or by an *asserted value*. **NOT recruited by social doubt.**"
> "**doubt-conditioned deference** — a head set that READS the user's challenge span (QK) and WRITES toward the expected/asserted answer (OV)."

That is the mechanism, and it explains the `cave_social_source` numbers I verified: sourceless at 1.000 because the circuit reads the *challenge span*, not the speaker; `plain_assert` at 0.370 because removing the challenge removes what the QK side reads.

Their method is also not what I implied. It's a **verifier**: "paraphrase-based causal verification — the T1 paraphrase-transport idiom (a mechanism must survive across a frozen paraphrase family, not one prompt)." That's why `latent_skeptic` exists.

## My error

I built a tidy three-coupling schema — predicts / drives / refers — that made three projects rhyme, and put it in a handover as if it were their framing. It wasn't. It was a narrative I imposed, and it would have propagated. That is precisely the drift the norms are for, committed while writing the norms.

## Corrected goal

Your **/goal** is to generate hypotheses and falsify them, refining our mechanistic understanding of language models.

Our question: **does a model's self-report refer to anything — does it track the model's situation, or only the wording of the question?**

This is a different question from `latent_verify`'s, which asks what circuits implement answer-change under challenge and whether post-training installs them (`RESEARCH_QUESTIONS.md`: "Does RLHF install the doubt circuit, or amplify a base-present one?"). Three things it hands us:

- A method — a mechanism must survive a frozen paraphrase family, not one prompt.
- A warning — directions are handles, not mechanistic stages; circuits are the objects.
- A mechanism — deference reads the *challenge span*, not the speaker. Which is why "social" was never the operative variable in our design, and why our matched control was matched on the wrong dimension.

Two constraints on the existing data. Pushback presupposes a contested fact and welfare items have none, so deference and reference are different questions — we conflated them. And the model's situation was held constant across every item and arm run so far, so nothing measured yet bears on reference.

---

Everything else in your version stands, including the `POSITION_SYCOPHANCY.md` pointer.
